title: Black-Hole Heart
summary: Keep stars orbiting the abyss at the center of the galaxy — and learn why the closest orbits are the fastest, the most precarious, and the highest-scoring.

intro.markdown: At the center of the Milky Way sits **Sagittarius A\*** (Sgr A\*), a **supermassive black hole** of about **4.3 million solar masses** packed into a region smaller than Mercury's orbit. This game puts you in charge of that heart: the single overwhelming mass is the black hole, the lethal black disk is its **event horizon**, and the glowing rings are its **accretion disk**. Your job is to keep stars in orbit on the very edge of the abyss.
**The core idea:** closer orbits are *faster*, more *precarious*, and worth *more* — exactly the tension that real astronomers exploit to weigh a black hole they can never see directly.

sections.title: The galaxy turns around a supermassive black hole
sections.intro: How we know a black hole is there at all — and what the game is really modeling.

steps.title: Meet Sagittarius A*
steps.objective: Know what sits at the galactic center and how its mass was measured.

body.markdown: We know Sgr A\*'s mass because we have watched stars — the **S-stars**, especially **S2** — sweep around it in tight, fast, decades-long orbits that only such a tiny, monstrous mass can produce. In 2022 the Event Horizon Telescope released the first image of the glowing ring around its shadow.

steps.title: The event horizon is a one-way door
steps.objective: Understand the radius of no return — the game's fail line.

body.markdown: Cross `r ≤ horizon` and the star is gone — swallowed, fed to the black hole, streak reset. The horizon is not a surface but the boundary inside which not even light can escape. Its size is the **Schwarzschild radius**:

body.caption: For Sgr A* this is roughly 12 million km — large for a star, vanishingly small for 4 million Suns.

sections.title: Why the mechanic teaches it (not just decorates it)
sections.intro: Every rule in the game maps onto real orbital physics.

body.markdown: Orbital speed is set by the mass and the radius. Halve the radius and the required speed rises by √2. The preview shows it — a tight orbit needs a much harder, more precise fling than a wide one.

body.caption: Bound orbital speed scales as v ∝ 1/√r.

body.markdown: Near a black hole gravity grows *faster* than Newton predicts, so close orbits **precess** — the ellipse itself rotates, exactly as S2's orbit precesses around Sgr A\* (measured by the GRAVITY instrument, confirming Einstein). Inside the **ISCO** (innermost stable circular orbit, at `3 r_s`) no stable circular orbit exists at all.
The most rewarding orbits in the game are the ones most likely to fall in — that risk/reward curve *is* the physics.

sections.title: What you should be able to say afterward

body.markdown:
- "Our galaxy has a supermassive black hole at its center — Sgr A\*, about 4 million Suns."
- "The event horizon is the point of no return; cross it and nothing comes back."
- "Closer orbits are faster — `v = √(GM/r)` — and near a black hole they precess and become unstable."
- "The glow is an accretion disk: gas heated white-hot as it slowly spirals in."

careers.title: Planetarium / science museum educator
careers.blurb: Runs the dome shows and exhibits that explain exactly this — black holes, orbits, the galactic center — to the public.
careers.background: Bachelor's in a science or education field; strong public-speaking; deep enthusiasm more than research credentials.

careers.title: Science communicator / journalist
careers.blurb: Turns results like the EHT image of Sgr A* into stories, videos, and articles people actually understand.
careers.background: Writing/media skills plus solid science literacy; a STEM degree helps but a portfolio matters more.

careers.title: Astrophysicist
careers.blurb: Studies the dynamics of stars and black holes — the people who tracked S2's orbit to weigh Sgr A*.
careers.background: PhD in physics or astronomy; years of math, coding, and observational or theoretical training.

careers.title: Data scientist (astronomy pipelines)
careers.blurb: Builds the software that turns telescope data into measured orbits and images — skills that transfer straight to industry.
careers.background: Strong programming + statistics; physics/CS degree; the most portable role on this list.

careers.title: Gravitational-wave analyst
careers.blurb: Hunts the spacetime ripples from merging black holes in LIGO/Virgo data — a field barely a decade old.
careers.background: Graduate-level general relativity and signal processing; strong background in physics and computation.

careers.title: Numerical-relativity researcher
careers.blurb: Simulates Einstein's equations on supercomputers to predict what merging black holes actually do.
careers.background: Deep expertise in general relativity, PDEs, and high-performance computing; research-level and esoteric.
